prompt.context: Your consulting firm has just signed a new client, Venture Golfing, a real estate company that specializes in buying premium tracts of land and transforming them into top-rated golf courses. To date they have only bought properties within the United States and Canada but are now looking to expand into other territories. In particular, they have been offered a large section of beachfront property on an independently governed Caribbean island. They are very interested in pursuing this opportunity but want your advice first.
prompt.question: Should Venture Golfing proceed with the acquisition of the Caribbean beachfront property or pass?

clarifying_info.a: It belongs to a world-renowned athlete looking to sell after 25 years of ownership. It consists of 15 acres of mostly beachfront property.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition on the island?
clarifying_info.a: The island only has one other golf course, which is in high demand but not rated very highly.

clarifying_info.q: What are the terms of the deal?
clarifying_info.a: The seller has agreed to allow Venture Golfing to option the property for six months. After this time, Venture Golf would either have to buy or relinquish their rights.
The island is non-union so labor costs are less than in the United States. There is a ready supply of water and food from several large resorts. Electricity is readily accessible and inexpensive.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any ownership or regulatory issues?
clarifying_info.a: Non-citizens are not permitted to own property. Foreign entities must work through a local title-holder. The property is zoned residential, not for a golf course. Government bureaucracy is notoriously slow — a zoning change petition could easily take over a year.
500-year-old ruins have been found on a neighboring lot. If any were uncovered during construction, all work would stop. However, ruins are uncommon and chances of finding any are slight.

The property neighbors four large residential lots owned by wealthy retirees who do not welcome construction. The only road connecting the property to the main highway runs through two neighboring properties; a new road would require going through one of them as well.

framework: Market attractiveness: assess demand for golf on the island and competitive landscape
Regulatory and legal feasibility: ownership restrictions, zoning requirements, timeline for changes
Construction and operational feasibility: costs, labor, utilities, access infrastructure
Risk assessment: environmental, neighbor opposition, road access, title-holder reliability
Financial viability: option cost, acquisition price, development cost vs. expected revenue
Go/no-go recommendation based on balance of feasibility, risk, and return

questions.prompt: What are the key regulatory obstacles and how do they affect the timeline?
questions.guidance: Strong answer highlights two blockers: (1) non-citizen ownership requires a local title-holder — takes time to find a reliable agent; (2) the property is zoned residential, not for a golf course — a zoning change petition can take over a year even without challenge. Since the option is only six months, the zoning issue alone makes it nearly impossible to close and begin development within the option window.

questions.prompt: What are the main risks beyond regulatory issues?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) Environmental risk — ruins on neighboring lot create precedent; if found on this property, construction halts entirely; (2) Neighbor opposition — four wealthy retirees nearby who are unfriendly to the idea; (3) Access risk — the only road runs through neighboring properties, and building a new road also requires a neighbor's cooperation; these social/physical constraints compound regulatory difficulty.

questions.prompt: Are there any favorable factors for this investment?
questions.guidance: Favorable factors include: only one competing golf course on the island (and it is low-rated), indicating unmet demand; non-union labor lowers construction costs; utilities and water supply are readily available from existing resorts; beachfront location is premium. However, candidate should note that these upsides are outweighed by the structural obstacles.

Recommend passing on the acquisition. The six-month option window is far too short to resolve a zoning change that could take over a year. Even if Venture Golf purchased the option, it would expire before the regulatory hurdle is cleared. Additional deal-breakers include limited road access (requiring neighbor cooperation), potential archaeological finds halting construction, and hostile neighbors who could create legal and political friction throughout the process.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Venture Golfing consider when evaluating any international real estate investment for a golf course?

categories.name: Market demand
ideas: Existing golf course capacity and ratings

categories.name: Regulatory and legal
ideas: Zoning classification and ease of change
Local permitting speed and corruption risk

categories.name: Construction and operations
ideas: Labor availability and cost (union vs. non-union)

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Expected green fees and membership revenue

recommendation: Do NOT proceed with the acquisition.
The six-month option window is structurally incompatible with a zoning change process that could take over a year, making it impossible to secure the necessary permits before the option expires.
risks: Zoning change denied or delayed beyond the option period
Archaeological finds discovered during construction halt all work
Neighbors block or litigate road access, making the property effectively landlocked
Title-holder arrangement proves unreliable or exposes Venture Golf to legal risk
next_steps: If Venture Golf remains interested in Caribbean expansion, seek properties that are already zoned for commercial/recreational use
Conduct due diligence on other Caribbean islands with more favorable foreign ownership and zoning laws
Evaluate whether a longer option period (18-24 months) could be negotiated to accommodate the regulatory timeline — though neighbor and access issues remain
